extraction.name: Visual Genome
extraction.description: A dataset of images densely annotated with region descriptions, objects, attributes, relationships, scene graphs, and question-answer pairs to support comprehensive scene understanding.
extraction.creator: Ranjay Krishna; Yuke Zhu; Oliver Groth; Justin Johnson; Kenji Hata; Joshua Kravitz; Stephanie Chen; Yannis Kalantidis; Li-Jia Li; David A. Shamma; Michael S. Bemstein; Li Fei-Fei
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The dataset was collected and verified entirely by crowd workers on Amazon Mechanical Turk. Workers created region descriptions with bounding boxes, extracted objects, attributes, and relationships, wrote question-answer pairs, and verified annotations through majority voting or rapid judgments.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Manual Human Curator, Software Collection, Secondary Data analysis
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The images come from the intersection of MS-COCO and YFCC100M; annotations include freeform worker-generated texts such as region descriptions and question-answer pairs.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Objects, attributes, relationships, and noun phrases in region descriptions and QAs were canonicalized to WordNet synsets using Stanford NLP tools, morphology normalization for attributes, sentence-frame matching for relationships, hand-crafted mapping rules, and AMT verification of mappings.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Crowd workers on AMT annotated images by drawing bounding boxes and writing region descriptions, extracting objects and grounding them with boxes, adding attributes and relationships to form region graphs, merging region graphs into scene graphs, writing freeform and region-based QA pairs, and verifying annotations via majority voting or rapid judgments.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Annotations were verified using majority voting with three workers for most components and rapid judgments for objects; an annotation was kept if at least two of three workers marked it correct.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Over 33,000 unique workers contributed; 93.02% were from the United States, with age and gender distributions reported, including a near-balanced split of 54.15% male and 45.85% female workers.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: Stanford dependency parser; Stanford NLP tools
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The dataset is somewhat biased toward images of people, and certain sports are overrepresented due to image source bias.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Canonicalization mappings are imperfect and still contain ambiguity; some descriptions contain no objects and therefore no region graphs; the image set is somewhat biased toward people.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended for training and benchmarking computer vision models for comprehensive scene understanding, including dense image captioning, visual question answering, image understanding evaluation, relationship extraction, and semantic image retrieval.

rai:dataCollectionRawData.evidence: The Visual Genome dataset consists of all 108 ;249 images from the intersection of MS-COCO's (Lin et al., 2014) 328 ;000 images and YFCC's (Thomee et al., 2016) 100 million images. All the descriptions and QAs that we collect are freeform worker-generated texts.

rai:dataCollectionTimeframe.evidence: The dataset was collected over the course of 6 months after 15 months of experimentation and iteration on the data representation.

rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol.evidence: In order to reduce the ambiguity in the concepts of our dataset and connect it to other resources used by the research community, we map all objects, attributes, relationships, and noun phrases in region descriptions and QAs to synsets in WordNet (Miller, 1995). We use the Stanford NLP tools (Manning et al., 2014) to extract the noun phrases from the region descriptions and QAs. We normalize each attribute based on morphology (so called "stemming") and map them to the WordNet adjectives. For relationships, we ignore all prepositions as they are not recognized by WordNet.

rai:dataAnnotationProtocol.evidence: When a new image is added to the crowdsourcing pipeline with no annotations, it is sent to a worker who is asked to draw three bounding boxes and write three descriptions for the region enclosed by each box. Each description is sent to one crowd worker, who extracts all the objects from the description and grounds each object as a bounding box in the image. We present each worker with a region description along with its extracted objects and ask them to add attributes to objects or to connect pairs of objects with relationships, based on the text of the description. To create question answer (QA) pairs, we ask the AMT workers to write pairs of questions and answers about an image. All Visual Genome data go through a verification stage as soon as they are annotated.

rai:dataAnnotationPlatform.evidence: We used Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT) as our primary source of annotations.

rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis.evidence: Verification is conducted using two separate strategies: majority voting (Snow et al., 2008) and rapid judgments (Krishna et al., 2016). Majority voting (Snow et al., 2008) involves three unique workers looking at each annotation and voting on whether it is factually correct. An annotation is added to our dataset if at least two (a majority) out of the three workers verify that it is correct.

rai:personalSensitiveInformation.evidence: Table 2 outlines the percentage distribution of the locations of the workers. The majority of our workers were between the ages of 25 and 34 years old. We also had a near-balanced split of 54:15% male and 45 :85% female workers.

rai:dataBiases.evidence: Our dataset is somewhat biased towards images of people, as Figure 13 shows; however, they are quite diverse overall. State-of-motion verbs ( standing ,walking ) are the most common, while certain sports ( skiing ,surfing ) are also highly represented due to an image source bias in our image set.

rai:dataLimitations.evidence: These mappings are not perfect and still contain some ambiguity.
